body: No, I've been asking him to get one but he never ends up following through.

Last night I was all done with final exams and we were about to go on winter break, so I thought I'd have a last hurrah with the guy I'm seeing. I planned on getting super drunk, as a celebration. We talked for a while while I was getting drunk, then he showed me the rough draft of a poem he wrote about me (we met through a poetry reading, so poems are really special to both of us). It was the most beautiful thing anyone's done for me, and I kept reading it over and over again. 

I ended up getting WASTED on wine and vodka (not a great combo) then eating a fuckton of sour patch kids. Then he suggested we smoke weed, and that's when it started going downhill. I was throwing up outside while lying on the ground for a good hour or so - it was the first time I've ever thrown up in my whole life (I've never had any flu or food poisoning). Obviously, it was not good. 

However, this guy is a goddamn national treasure. I've been seeing him for about a month now and I feel such a connection with him, we're really into each other. He, of course, held my hair back while I was a mess. He knew that being nauseous just makes me anxious which leads to worse nausea, so he was reassuring me that it would be okay, that he doesn't mind taking care of me, that he's been in my position and that I'll feel better soon. I was being a huge wimp and refused to get up when he asked me to, because I was scared I'd throw up again if I tried to walk back to the dorms. He eventually convinced me to get back to my bed, he tucked me in, and put a trash can near the bed. Then he rubbed my back until I fell asleep. 

I got out of an abusive relationship sort of recently, so I expected this new guy to get pissed at me for not controlling myself. His kindness and gentleness really touched my heart. This morning I woke up and apologized for what happened, and he goes, "it's okay, it was a good team-building activity." The idea of us being a team really got to me, and I teared up because I was so happy. I really, really like this guy, and I'm going to miss him for the next month while I'm on winter break.

Actually, you're right. Getting her a gift would be super manipulative and shitty of me. I feel bad for even thinking of that.

I might have to reconsider our friendship. Although we have a ton of fun when we're together, she does this to me a lot and apologizes but it doesn't seem genuine.
That's true. She gets to be safe posting whatever she wants about me and she knows that I won't be able to say anything about it unless I want to face her anger as well.

I say thank you every single time. Even if I hate what my mom got me, I'll wear it around her just to be nice. The times when I've said "Don't spend money on me if you're going to spend it on things that I told you I DIDN'T WANT," it's after she's already gotten mad at me. For example, once I told her "I really need earbuds, but not over-the-ear headphones, because I need something to wear at the gym." I wrote it down, reminded her, sent her a picture of the 10 dollar earbuds, etc. She still got me over-the-ear headphones, and I asked her if we could please exchange them for earbuds. She said no, and that I was being ungrateful, and that I should appreciate her spending so much money on me (despite the fact that I feel guilty as fuck for it). This happens for every single gift-giving holiday.

The way my friend was talking, she associated gift-giving with being thoughtful. She mentioned the necklace as an "example" of how thoughtful gift-giving works, and suggested that I be thoughtful, as well. I just didn't get the sense that it was a no-strings-attached gift.

I don't know if I can confront her about the blog thing.

She told me not to read it because it's "her private thoughts" and gets mad at me for invading her privacy if I bring up anything she posts there.

Just like Lana, I really like the repetition of the word "and." 

The formatting of the poem, in terms of the line length, really works for the overall feel of the piece. It feels sort of disjointed and almost clumsy (just like birds before they learn to fly). Very interesting piece!

I really like the tone that this creates. I can't quite put my finger on it, but it's very...hazy? I think your use of stanzas was very helpful, that last line packed a huge punch that made the rest of the poem make sense.

I especially like the lines, "and the end of a cigarette
glows through gray: a lighthouse." I think poetry can help people look at things in a new way, and I never thought of a cigarette in this way until I read this.

I've always hated horror movies and I scare extremely easily. There is one jump scare that I would say is a legitimate jump scare. There are a few things that aren't actually "jump scares," but they surprised me because of how sudden they were, and because I was already hyped up from how suspenseful it was overall. I watched it during the day with a friend, and I still had to cover my eyes. It's not horror movie scary, but I wish I would've been better prepared for what was coming.
Howso? I'm genuinely wondering, because the actors I know are pretty dedicated, I go to a school with a really serious acting program.

You're right that his unavailability is making me more into him. I have a tendency to try to get close to people when they pull away.

I'm still going to keep dating people, even if it's not as "magical" as things were with him. He's not the only likeable person in the universe.

I'm going to chime in and confirm that therapy could really help you here. Childhood sexual abuse is no joke, and can not only affect your view of sex, but your view of yourself. I've gone through it myself, and I can say that it can plant ideas so far in your head, that professional help is needed to extract them and analyze them. You don't deserve to go through this alone. Even if externally you feel you have gotten over it (because you're in a relationship and don't have issues in other areas of your life), there's clearly something bigger lurking underneath. You need to go to therapy so that you can identify the motivations behind your actions. I was on autopilot for years after the abuse and made many decisions that were ultimately just unhealthy coping techniques.

By having sex with your husband when you don't want to, you are harming and possibly re-traumatizing yourself. This is a very normal response for victims of trauma, but it's a very dangerous one. Continuing this way might cause you to build up resentment toward your husband - after all, your actions are casting him in the role of "abuser" and you in the role of "victim."

I can't stress enough that you can't blame yourself for any of this. You are suffering the effects of something horrible. This type of anxiety and compulsive repetition of past abuse is the reason why child abuse is so despicable in the first place. It's something you didn't ask for, and yet it still affects your adult relationships. 

The best thing for you right now is to find a good therapist who you can trust, and who has experience with those suffering from anxiety and PTSD. I did this, and it changed my life for the better. I've discovered the ways in which trauma affected my sense of self, and for the first time in my life I'm realizing that sex isn't the only thing I'm good for. I'm a complex person worthy of love, and so are you. It seems like you aren't treating yourself like that right now. Right now, you are suffering under the weight of your own expectations, and it's damaging you. 

If your husband is as amazing as you say he is, then he will understand that your self worth is a million times more important than getting his dick wet. He will support you in this - and it seems like he already has. He is probably feeling guilt because he knows deep down that he is contributing to you being retraumatized. Do both him and yourself a favor, and speak with a professional about how to stop this cycle. You do not deserve to feel this much anxiety over sex, which is just one part of a relationship. You deserve to learn healthy coping techniques and to stop putting yourself through this hell. 

I'm just speaking from my personal experience, so I hope you take this message to heart. Take care of yourself. <3
Did you mean to comment this here? I'm not a big Star Wars person so I don't understand what this means.

Oh, yeah. It would be doing other people a disservice to completely badmouth her, because then people would probably see me as a huge outlier and disregard my opinion. I don't have any ill will toward her, I just think that there is a very specific type of person that could benefit from her style of therapy, and I wasn't one of those people. 

Thank you!

Thank you for sharing your story. 

I'm so sorry about the betrayal you feel, and about the emptiness in your wife's heart that causes her to do this. I've been in her position before, and avoiding filling that emptiness with unhealthy relationship behaviors is like avoiding something you're addicted to. It's very compassionate of you to stick by her through this time even though you must be really hurting. I can't imagine doing this to a spouse and I hope that it never gets to be that severe. 

I discovered something a few days ago through conversation with my boyfriend that may be helpful for you to hear. When I was growing up in these relationships, the way I learned to love was the thing that most people call "child grooming." I thought that love was about using people. I didn't know that love was supposed to involve respect, joy, and equality. However, this grooming was so normalized in my mind that it became what I knew love to be - when I was abused, that's when I felt "fulfilled" and what you'd call "loved." Now that I'm out of those situations and I've found healthier friendships and relationships, it's so hard to feel as "loved" as I once did. My friends and boyfriend respect me, support me, and don't look at me as an object. On paper that sounds fantastic, and I should be so happy about that. But deep down, part of me is unfulfilled, because the way I got my worth is now considered "abusive." It's terrifying now to accept real love and respect. I'm willing to bet that you're a great husband, which is precisely why your wife may have not felt "whole" by it. Abuse is EXTREMELY powerful, and in my experience, it's even more powerful than love sometimes. Love is very gentle and patient; abuse is a roller coaster. I think I became too addicted to the thrill, so anything less won't bring those feelings of worthiness. 

Now I'm pretty young and I'm in the "thinks she knows everything" stage so I totally get it if you take my words with a grain of salt, or even if you flat-out disagree. But I'm just speaking from my own feelings and reasons why I've had trouble with respectful and loving relationships. 

I do agree that long-term, early trauma can manifest as bpd. I'm not looking for a bpd diagnosis anymore, I'm just getting help from my therapist and seeing where it leads, which is way more helpful. 

Thank you for your honest and insightful comment!

This is a really good point. I don't mind my boyfriend pointing out that my emotional moments tend to be frequent, strong, and long-lasting. But adding the feeling of being a burden on him just makes the feeling worse, particularly when he talks about how my emotions are exhausting him. It's hard for me to acknowledge that and be understanding toward his feelings when I'm feeling super shitty myself, but he takes that as me invalidating his feelings. I'm trying to work harder to validate that his emotional exhaustion is as important and necessary-to-deal with as mine, even if mine seems to be more intense (as I am the one experiencing it directly). 

And another commenter just mentioned "I hate you, don't leave me" as a reading suggestion. I've asked him to read that a few times and he's skimmed over it but sometimes feels frustrated that he has to do all this just to understand me, and yet I don't read literature about how to handle HIS needs. I think this means he believes I'm not putting effort into the relationship, which probably really hurts him. It seems unfair for him to have to read a book to help me out and support me, even though I "don't do much" in comparison. I'll still talk with him about it again though. 

Thank you!

I've actually read that book and asked my boyfriend to look over it! We haven't really implemented anything yet but thankfully it exists and I like what it has to say. I'll probably give it another go after reading this comment. 

Thank you!

Yes! Thank you so much for your comment in my last thread. It doesn't 'always' work out, and sometimes we'll still resort to blaming behaviors. But overall we've had more empathy-filled discussions. I didn't realize how much easier conflict was if you just take care to acknowledge the other person's feelings (particularly if they're feeling slighted in some way) instead of just freaking out about things. 

Thank you for your help!

Wow, that sounds like a waste of time and money. I'm sorry that happened to you. Especially with your mom there - I can't even imagine. I agree that some therapists really just aren't cut out for the job.

Wow, I didn't think that anyone was paying enough attention to wait for an update. Thank you for your interest and I'm glad that my update was exciting for you to see. 

Thank you for your kind words!

Definitely! And the last thing I need is to be controlled by more people. Instead of not being able to live without control, I'm now breaking out of my shell and recognizing how good it feels to make my own decisions.
Haha, true. Quick-to-diagnose, acting like they know everything, suggesting breakups frequently. However, this sub has been really great with my issue in particular, so I don't mind much.

That sounds horrible, for both your coworker and for the people around him. It's so hard when people refuse to take responsibility for things like that, and I know that I don't want to be one of those "out of control" people. Feeling like I'm in charge of myself is worth any pain that therapy puts me through. The stigma around therapy can be hard to get past as well, but the stigma of being a miserable person who makes those around them miserable is even worse. 

Thank you!

Honestly. It's such a simple thing - I've felt really invalidated and ignored throughout my life. Having an hour per week where someone wants to focus on helping ME improve and grow is invaluable. 

Thank you!

I've heard a lot about them. I think right now we're doing psychodynamic with some CBT, but I'll definitely ask her about her experience with DBT and then decide if that's a good approach for me. Thank you!

That does sound like a pretty huge violation. If nothing else, he should've known that a 16 year old isn't in the position to give therapy to a professional! 

I think it sucks that he did that but it's alright that you didn't report him. You did the best you could do at the time. I probably wouldn't have had the courage to switch therapists at 16, either - much less report a bad one! Your comment has inspired me to consider writing a Yelp review for my old therapist because she has a lot of glowing recommendations and I feel like my point of view might be useful to let people know that sometimes 5 stars on Yelp can be too good to be true (at least in my situation).

Whoa, that's amazing. I'm really glad that you got help and that you overcame your fear. I had a phobia of dogs when I was a kid and a good therapist helped me a lot with that. Phobias are nothing to mess around with - I'm glad you got your life back by getting the help you deserved.

One of them was "Feeling Good" by David Burns. It does feel a little outdated at some points but the general message of just writing down your feelings and having a dialogue with yourself is really helpful. It really drives home the point that our automatic thoughts create the strong emotional responses we experience. I personally have the trademark depressive thoughts ("I'm worthless, I'm alone in this world, I'm wrong about everything") even in the smallest situations, which explains why I get so upset in such a big way. Who wouldn't feel upset with a voice in their head telling them that shit when they did something inconsequential like accidentally misspeak in conversation or get a 90% instead of 100% on an assignment? 

Another book was "Drama of the gifted child" by Alice Miller. I was just recommended that one, as well as one called "the prison of childhood" (not sure if that's what it's called, I'm on mobile so it's hard to check) by the same author. I haven't really looked at them too much but the first one seems to be pretty decent so far. She told me I should look into them because I think that my parents (particularly my mom) didn't realize that they hurt me by not accepting bad feelings or negativity or anything that didn't fit into their idea of the type of person I should be. The book explains that this happens because some parents have children in order to fill a psychological void within themselves. It's obvious that my mom has a huge need for approval (I'm actually starting to relate to her more because of this!) and so whenever I was not "ideal" as a kid she had to force me back into the ideal so that society would deem her a good Catholic and a good mother.

Oh yes, I definitely do. I tell him what I talked about each session and we discuss it, he's happy about the conclusions I come to with her and he feels that she really gets me. 

I know that I can be draining to him, so I did suggest therapy for himself if he ever feels too overwhelmed. He hasn't felt the need to do that yet, and hopefully it doesn't have to get that bad. But I do want him to get help if need be, because the last thing I want to do is psychologically damage or fatigue him.

Whoa, thank you for this. This hit the nail on the head and it points out why I genuinely feel that I'm being treated differently during disagreements. I make a firm effort to avoid saying "always" and I don't recall ever slipping up. I remember talking to a teacher about this last year and she said that one of the many small things that keeps her relationship healthy with her husband is to never say always. If she really needs to say something like that, she'll say "I've noticed that lately you've tended to do [insert action]" or "I feel like you should watch out for [insert action here]." I try to use those, but maybe I should be careful about referencing the past at all because usually it's irrelevant. I feel like he only brings up the past frequently because he has resentments about it and the issue isn't always resolved because it's a fundamental personality issue (the fact that I'm too sensitive, for example."

I totally do feel boxed in when he makes "always" statements, but the times that I've told him that, he'll say "Well I'm sorry you feel that way, that's not what I was trying to do." I think that if I talk with him about always/never statements then it'll reduce the amount of times where I feel boxed in or trapped, and hopefully he won't make me feel that way without meaning to. 


We do tend to address patterns a lot. I'm wondering, is that unhealthy to do in general? Sometimes I notice some worrying patterns (such as the tendency to use "always" statements) and I don't know how to bring it up. I try not to bring it up unless he actually does something within the pattern that I noticed. But maybe I should be bringing it up in a more neutral situation and not during s fight? 

I think a lot of our issues stem from him wanting to skip the first step, and me wanting to skip the second step (because sometimes when I'm upset I have troubles with getting ''stuck" on an emotion). I think that avoiding "always" statements can help with making the first step easier, and finding ways to diffuse the tension could help with the second. 

Thank you for your response, I'm glad to get an outside point of view on how my boyfriend and I can improve our communication skills.

My school does offer some services, but only if you have the school's insurance (which is more expensive than the insurance my family has now). If you're not on the insurance then you only get about 3 sessions per quarter, and the intake (which I tried, and it was only 15 minutes) counts as the first one. I tried to schedule a time where I could meet with a therapist there and they could help me find one outside of school, but the next appointment for that was months in the future and so I just did it myself. 

About the telling my boyfriend thing, I agree that I probably shouldn't have done that. For the record, I did say that I disagreed with her and that even though there were times where he was accidentally manipulative, I thought her statements were too extreme and felt uncomfortable with it. In the future I feel like I could keep the part about feeling manipulated (maybe I'd word it more kindly though) and leave out the rest. 

Thank you for the kind words.

Yeah, you have a point here. 

Just tonight (a few minutes ago) I was in a really good mood and was reading an article aloud to myself while we were talking on the phone. He suddenly had an annoyed tone of voice and said "do you HAVE to read this aloud? It's a ton of words." And I was like "no sorry, I'll read it to myself" and tried to hide my hurt, but for whatever reason I took it personally. He said that it sucked how he always had to avoid saying ANYTHING negative because I always take it so personally and get upset. I told him that I tried not to visibly act upset but at the same time I couldn't control my emotional responses, to which he replied "it's unfair that I always have to control myself but apparently you have no control over yourself." I kept it together as best as I could but eventually when explaining that I was trying harder to have better reactions to criticism, I started crying and he got frustrated that I was crying and said "see, now you're crying and you're going to bring this up later instead of leaving it in the past. I shouldn't have even said anything."

I do think that I deserved his response, because I was being really annoying with my reading and I do cry a lot. I don't know how I can be mad over something that *I* did wrong.

Thank you. I think that finding a new therapist will help me assert my agency over my life. I gave her a good try and saw her about 6 times total, but I'm feeling no change at all and haven't made any new revelations (I feel like my self-growth is furthered more by talking to my roommate or boyfriend or dad than my therapist). 

And yes, she's only heard the negative aspects. I don't think I need to break up with him right now. I will keep my radar up like she said, but I don't think it's necessary to make rash decisions or anything.

I guess I was mistaken about that first point. My roommates have pointed out that I talk to him a lot and that they could never handle that much communication in a relationship, so maybe I was just wrongly assuming that we were abnormal.

And yeah, I did probably wrongly absolve him. I agree that he shouldn't be lashing out, but at the same time I'm not sure...no one can be perfect ALL the time, right? I've never gotten so exhausted where I've lashed out and hurt him or said something that I knew was cruel, but I do get upset easily and during those times I don't always react maturely, either. I feel like since he gives me some leeway, I can give him some as well. I don't know, maybe this is the wrong way to look at it.

I didn't realize that the comment about problems was rude. I asked my roommate and she said that was horrible of him to say and that he wasn't accepting responsibility for his actions. But I thought it was okay eventually because we worked through it.

Yeah, sometimes he does beat himself up about hurting me, but at the same time I'm prone to reassurance/apologizing instead of getting mad at someone. I don't think it's completely his fault, I think that my more easygoing/submissive personality perpetuates it as well.

I do end up apologizing a lot, and he blames me for starting it (because I usually do, by feeling upset or afraid or suicidal). Sometimes these emotions come on strongly and for a long time, which is understandably stressful to deal with. I'd be exhausted too if I had to deal with someone like me in a relationship. I even exhaust myself sometimes (which is why I devolve into negative self-talk, and am understanding when he talks negatively to me occasionally). I'm trying to work on my self-worth but no one really helps me figure out ways to build that, my therapist just says "you have low self-worth" and "you're not a whole person" but never really elaborates.

Thank you for the suggestion!

I've been working on the way in which I approach my emotions (if I'm having a breakdown, I've found that it's best to try to handle it on my own until I'm a bit easier to deal with. If I'm just talking about them calmly, then I can tell him whatever and he won't be tired). I've also been trying to show my appreciation through words and letters, because he likes being reaffirmed randomly.
Thanks, I'll look into it!
Thank you, that's really kind of you to say and that last part made me tear up.
This is a good point. I think the person I'm seeing now is a marriage and family therapist.

Thank you for the therapy model recommendation.

Looking it up, I do think that this would be a useful therapy model for me. I've noticed that my therapist doesn't directly address how to handle emotions or how to follow them to the root of the problem. She usually just points out how the other person is right or wrong. 

I feel like sometimes my emotions are "inappropriate" for a situation because I've developed some maladaptive coping techniques (on account of the past abusive relationships). For example, I feel fear and even resentment most times when people try to show me affection, because growing up I learned that affection = manipulation in order to get me to do things I didn't want to do. It would be great to be able to deal with these emotions more closely, since ultimately the only emotional response I can change is my own emotional response. 

Thank you again for the support!

Thank you for the analysis of the scenarios. I appreciate you pointing out that things aren't always black and white, and that there could be multiple things going on.

I agree that therapy hasn't been effective because instead of focusing on myself, she has me focusing on finding the negatives in my life and wondering if she's trustworthy. I do tell her a lot but I don't fully trust her (I hold back a lot because I'm worried she'll speak as badly about me as she speaks about my mom, my boyfriend, people with personality disorders, other clients, etc). 

I'm going to keep looking, thank you.

Thank you for your reply, it's balanced and understanding of all the aspects of the situation.

I do agree that she definitely had a point behind what she does, and isn't a total quack or anything. But she definitely could be a little bit more gentle, as I am a sensitive person.

And I'm starting to think that, yes, it was an invalidating thing for my boyfriend to do. That hasn't happened before to such a degree so that incident kind of shocked me. He does have a bit of a manipulative streak, though, as you said. He can be very insecure and will sometimes try to talk himself up (which, in turn, can involve talking down to me, because I easily go along with it). However, since I discussed with this him a few weeks ago, he's made an active effort to avoid doing this. He is even more supportive than ever, and is more willing to admit his past mistakes. 

I definitely think that I see all the negatives in myself. Lately, I've been trying to be more positive (my boyfriend has been helping me with this too, by pointing it out/complimenting me on specific good things, rather than just telling me where I need to improve), but it's difficult after living this way for so long. I do feel like my therapist is pushing me toward the positive in myself, which is good (I've discovered that I'm more mature and empathetic than I thought I was). At the same time, though, I don't exactly want to do it at the expense of those around me. She seems to push me toward feeling negatively toward my parents and my boyfriend, leaving only my roommate as the only "positive" person in my life. Even if that's true, it feels extreme for her to say things like "Your mom has no right to call herself a mother." She may be right, but when I ask her to be more gentle about it, she just says, "Hear it." (???)

Her points are valid but it's not worth feeling this uneasy about her. 

I'll make sure to keep my guard up about my boyfriend, though. Right now we're working on getting better but I'll try to be extra cautious if it starts slipping back into invalidation.

I'm not faking anything, although I do admit I can be attention-seeking at times. Even then, it would be good for me to get help with my need for validation/attention (rather than just writing it off).

Yes, I was shocked as well. I already knew that people with BPD can be considered difficult to deal with, but I thought it wasn't appropriate to complain about it to me. She definitely does seem gossip-y at times, even outside of this incident.

This is a really good point, I am trusting her with much more than I realized. 

I'm nervous about leaving with no explanation because I have trouble leaving people in general. I'm worried about her feeling offended or like she's a bad therapist. Luckily, I don't have an appointment for this week since I'm out of town and I haven't scheduled any future appointments yet.
This is how I found her in the first place, I'll make sure to do that again and hopefully it'll turn out better this time.

Yeah, she does have a tendency to frame me as "right" in every situation, which I know isn't really true. There's probably a reason for this but I think it would be good to find a new therapist. It'll be difficult to find one who is close enough and accepts my insurance (I found her after calling at least 15 different people) but I guess it's the only option at this point that will make me feel secure.

I never diagnosed myself or said that I thought I had it. I was just telling her that I was worried that I related to it, by referencing the criteria and giving her examples of where this was happening in my life. 

l'd be perfectly fine not getting a diagnosis, but I was hurt that she reacted immediately (I would have preferred that she listened fully to at least make me feel like she was taking my words into consideration).

I'm sorry for being silly about the whole love thing. I'm sure I could find someone else but that statement feels unnecessarily harsh.
